description: Welcome to Team SpaceByte! Based in Colombo, we're a team passionate about computer systems engineering, space exploration, and solving complex off-world challenges. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are tackling the Martian Map challenge to design intuitive visualization tools for planetary survival. Looking for developers, designers, and space enthusiasts to build something incredible with us!
summary:
Our team developed Jezero Field Atlas, an interactive tool for exploring Mars terrain and planning simulated astronaut traverses across Jezero Crater. It uses USGS elevation data to identify steep terrain and calculate routes between science waypoints. Users can compare routes by distance, ascent, and maximum slope, explore mineral and thermal inertia layers, and preview or export their mission plan.

The project turns planetary data into practical exploration decisions. By showing where steep terrain affects a route, the atlas helps users weigh travel distance against slope and access to science targets.

For a future version, we propose transferring the planned route, waypoints, and terrain hazard map to an astronaut’s wrist-mounted display before a surface excursion. The display could show the next waypoint and nearby steep terrain at a glance, with an offline copy of the route available throughout the traverse.
details:
Our team built Jezero Field Atlas, an interactive map and traverse planner for simulated astronaut missions in Jezero Crater. Users can load a GeoTIFF, place science waypoints, and calculate a route across the terrain. The map shows elevation, contours, and steep slopes. Optional mineral and thermal inertia layers add context when choosing which locations to explore.

The route planner uses the A* search algorithm and a 20-meter USGS elevation model. It checks the slope between neighboring cells, avoids gaps in the elevation data, and applies slope limits based on the selected route profile. Users can compare routes by distance, ascent, and maximum slope, then preview the traverse or export the mission plan as JSON. We built the interface with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and used Python, Rasterio, and NumPy to process the terrain data and calculate routes.

We designed the atlas to make the trade-offs of surface exploration visible. A shorter route can cross steeper terrain, while a gentler route may take longer or change which science stops fit into the traverse. We also considered the limits of the source data. A 20-meter grid can reveal larger slopes, while smaller hazards such as individual rocks may fall below its resolution.

For a future version, we propose transferring the planned route, waypoints, and mapped hazards to an astronaut’s wrist-mounted display before a surface excursion. The display could keep an offline copy of the plan and show the next waypoint, the direction to travel, and nearby steep terrain at a glance. This concept connects the planning tool to the moment an astronaut needs to find their way in the field.
dataRefs: THEMIS-derived Thermal Inertia of Jezero Crater, Mars
